key_facts: **Dermatophyte** infection of keratin (stratum corneum, hair, nails), mostly *Trichophyton rubrum*.
**Asymmetrical** annular plaque with a scaly **active edge** and central clearing; tinea pedis causes macerated toe webs.
Scrape the **edge** for microscopy if uncertain, extensive or before oral treatment.
Topical terbinafine or an imidazole **until 1–2 weeks after clearance**; treat feet and nails (the reservoir).
A topical steroid alone causes **tinea incognito**.

sections.title: Overview

head: Form
Plain definition
rows: Dermatophyte infection of the groin (‘jock itch’)
Athlete’s foot: interdigital, moccasin or vesicular

blocks: All three are caused by **dermatophytes**, most often *Trichophyton rubrum*. They are **contagious**, spreading by spores and fomites (towels, floors, clothing) and from animals.

blocks.h4: Tinea manuum and pedis on the palms and soles (Module 3 Week 6)

ul: dermatophyte infection of the hand (tinea manuum — much less common) and foot (tinea pedis — very common). Usual organisms *Trichophyton rubrum*, *T. interdigitale*, *Epidermophyton floccosum*; zoophilic (*Microsporum canis*, *T. verrucosum*, *T. erinacei*) cause inflamed lesions.

sub: Worldwide, especially hot humid climates; tinea pedis affects up to 15–25% of adults at some point.
Tinea corporis is most common in **children and young adults**; tinea cruris and pedis in adult **men**.
Skin-to-skin contact, shared towels, bedding and changing rooms; animals (*Microsporum canis* from cats and dogs, *T. verrucosum* from cattle).

sections.title: Aetiology: causes and risk factors
blocks: Dermatophytes are keratin-loving fungi that invade the **stratum corneum** (and hair and nails). The infection spreads outwards in a ring, which produces the **active edge with central clearing**.
**Autoinoculation** is common: infection spreads from the feet and nails to the groin and body.

ul: **Risk factors:** occlusion, sweating, sport, shared towels and changing rooms.
**Pets and farm animals:** zoophilic species cause more inflamed, pustular lesions.

blocks.title: Tinea cruris risk factors (Module 5)
blocks.text: Hot, humid weather; sweating and sport; tight, occlusive clothing; **diabetes**; and immunosuppression. The usual organism is *T. rubrum*, with *T. interdigitale* and *Epidermophyton floccosum* also seen.

blocks.title: Why steroids make tinea worse
blocks.text: A topical steroid suppresses the local immune response that is holding the fungus back. The redness fades, but the dermatophyte spreads freely. The result is **tinea incognito**: a larger, less scaly, atypical rash that is easily mistaken for eczema.

ul: **Organisms**: anthropophilic *T. rubrum* (most common), *T. interdigitale*, *T. tonsurans*; zoophilic *M. canis*, *T. verrucosum*, *T. erinacei* (hedgehogs) give more inflamed lesions.
**Medical risk factors**: previous tinea, **diabetes**, immunosuppression, hyperhidrosis, obesity, ichthyosis.
**Environment**: occlusive footwear and clothing, sport, crowding, pets, contact sports (tinea gladiatorum).
Emerging **sexually transmitted** *T. mentagrophytes* genotype VII and **terbinafine-resistant** *T. indotineae* (extensive, recalcitrant groin and body tinea, often after travel to South Asia).
**"Any ring is ringworm"**: granuloma annulare, discoid eczema and others make rings; scrape if unsure.
**"Stop once it looks clear"**: continue for 1–2 weeks after clearance or it relapses.
**"A combined steroid cream is best"**: steroid-antifungal is a short bridge only (up to 7 days) for very inflamed skin.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: Dermatophytes live only in **dead keratin**; the shape of the rash reflects how they spread and how the host reacts.

mech.t: Spores from people, animals, soil or fomites stick to keratinocytes, helped by warmth, moisture and minor trauma.
Fungi release **keratinases** and proteases to invade the **stratum corneum**, hair and nail; they rarely go deeper because of serum inhibitory factors and host immunity.
mech.caption: Dermatophyte hyphae spread only through the dead outer layer (stratum corneum), releasing keratin-digesting enzymes; immune cells gather beneath.

mech.t: Hyphae grow outwards, while the host's inflammatory response clears the centre: an **active scaly edge with central clearing**.
mech.caption: The ring grows outwards: the most active fungus is at the scaly edge, which is where to scrape.

mech.t: Strong cell-mediated immunity (often zoophilic species) gives inflamed, pustular lesions; weak responses (*T. rubrum*, immunosuppression, steroid use) give chronic, widespread, less inflamed disease (**tinea incognito**).
Feet and nails act as reservoirs; scratching and towels spread fungus to the groin and body (**autoinoculation**).

histo: Fungal hyphae in the stratum corneum (seen with PAS or Grocott stain), sometimes the 'sandwich sign' between orthokeratotic and parakeratotic layers.
Mild spongiosis and a superficial perivascular infiltrate; neutrophils in the stratum corneum.
In practice, diagnosis is by **skin scrapings** (microscopy with KOH and culture or PCR), not biopsy.

sections.title: Clinical features
blocks: One or more **asymmetrical annular** plaques with an active red, scaly, advancing edge and central clearing. Usually itchy.

ul: **Tinea incognito:** altered by steroid, so less scaly and more widespread.
**Majocchi granuloma:** a deeper, follicular infection, often after shaving or steroid use.
**Kerion-like inflammation:** boggy and pustular, typical of zoophilic species.

blocks: Affects the inguinal folds, with or without the inner thighs. The scaly edge may be less obvious in moist folds. The **scrotum is usually spared**, whereas **Candida often involves it**.

Tinea cruris often starts on **one side or asymmetrically**. It can spread to the thighs and buttocks, and sometimes has vesicles at the active edge. The scrotum is usually spared, but this is a teaching rule rather than an absolute one.

ul: **Interdigital:** maceration, peeling and fissures between the toes, especially the 4th–5th web space.
**Moccasin:** dry, hyperkeratotic scaling of the sole and side of the foot.
**Vesicobullous:** inflamed vesicles on the instep.

blocks.h: Tinea manuum and pedis on the palms and soles (Module 3 Week 6)

ul: **Clues:** **"two feet–one hand" syndrome** (hyperkeratotic scale on one palm + both soles); **white scale accentuating creases** (vs red lichenified creases in eczema); asymmetric; spread contiguous from palm to dorsum with a raised edge; **nails** (onychomycosis); toe-web maceration; moccasin scaling of soles. Risk: manual work, hyperhidrosis, pre-existing hand eczema, animal/soil contact.
**Steroid trap:** topical steroid alters appearance (tinea incognito) — scrape before treating any unexplained unilateral palm rash.

bodymap.caption: Where tinea shows up: scalp, rings on the trunk and limbs, both groin folds onto the inner thighs, and the feet. Always check the feet and nails.

sub: Edges may look grey, violaceous or hyperpigmented rather than red; post-inflammatory pigmentation is common.
Tinea corporis and capitis are commonest; check pets and family members.
Treat tinea pedis promptly: fissured toe webs are a portal for cellulitis.

ul: Clinical pattern plus risk factors.

Take **skin scrapings from the active edge** for microscopy, with or without culture, if: the diagnosis is uncertain, treatment has failed, before starting oral antifungals, for extensive disease, or if immunocompromised.
**Always examine the feet, nails and hands** when the groin or body is involved.
Swab the folds if bacterial co-infection is suspected.

ddx.f: Sharp salmon-pink, no scale in folds, other sites.

ul: Keep the skin clean and **dry**, especially the toe webs and folds. Wear loose cotton clothing.
Do not share towels. Wash clothing and bedding hot.
Treat any foot or nail infection at the same time.
Children with body or groin tinea do **not** usually need to be kept off school (CKS).
Topical **terbinafine**, or an imidazole (**clotrimazole, miconazole, econazole**). Continue for **1–2 weeks after the skin looks clear**.
If very inflamed, add a mild steroid (e.g. hydrocortisone 1%) for a **maximum of 7 days**. **Never use a steroid alone.**
Adults: oral **terbinafine** first line, ideally after sending scrapings. Alternatives are itraconazole and griseofulvin.
Children with extensive disease: refer to paediatric dermatology.
Same topical classes. **Allylamines (terbinafine)** are often preferred for dermatophytes.
Advise on drying the toe webs and on footwear. Treat onychomycosis through its separate pathway.
Consider oral therapy if severe, if topicals fail, or if immunocompromised. Check LFTs and interactions for terbinafine and itraconazole.

blocks.h: Tinea manuum and pedis on the palms and soles (Module 3 Week 6)

ul: tinea pedis — topical **terbinafine 1%** (1–2 weeks) or an imidazole (clotrimazole/miconazole, ~4 weeks); foot hygiene, dry webs, change socks, treat shoes. Tinea manuum (hyperkeratotic palm) often needs **oral terbinafine** (adult 250 mg daily, typically 2–6 weeks) after mycology confirmation; check LFTs/drug interactions per BNF; treat feet/nails simultaneously to prevent re-infection. Refer if diagnosis uncertain or immunosuppressed.

blocks.title: Prescribing limits and pitfalls
list: **Steroid alone**: Never: it creates tinea incognito.
**Combinations**: Steroid–antifungal is a short bridge only (up to 7 days).
**Azoles**: Watch CYP interactions with oral itraconazole and fluconazole.

refer.t: Tinea pedis in **diabetes** or past cellulitis: fissured webs are an entry point.
Immunocompromised with extensive or atypical disease; children needing oral treatment.
Failure despite adherence: scrape and reconsider; occupational or institutional outbreak.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: Diagnostic doubt, or failure despite good adherence: take scrapings and reconsider.
**Kerion** or **Majocchi granuloma**, or suspected deep infection.
Immunocompromised patient with extensive or atypical disease.
Children needing oral treatment.
Occupational or institutional outbreak.
Tinea pedis in a person with diabetes or a history of cellulitis: fissured toe webs are an **entry point for cellulitis**.
Spread to other sites and household contacts.
**Bacterial superinfection** and cellulitis through fissured toe webs.
**Majocchi granuloma** (follicular invasion, often after steroid use) and **kerion** (scalp).
Id (dermatophytide) reaction: itchy vesicles at a distant site.
Chronic dermatophytosis (T. rubrum at 4 or more sites) and resistant infection.
Usually cured with correct treatment and adherence.
Relapse is common if treatment stops too early or reservoirs (feet, nails, contacts, pets) are not treated.

pearls: Always look at the **feet** in a ‘groin rash’.
A steroid–antifungal combination is a **short bridge only** (up to 7 days). Explain why steroid on its own is harmful.
**Oral terbinafine:** check interactions and LFTs if used for a prolonged period. Taste disturbance is uncommon but worth mentioning.
**Azoles:** watch for CYP interactions, especially with oral itraconazole and fluconazole.
OTC clotrimazole and terbinafine are widely available and are a good first pharmacy intervention for limited tinea.
**Recurrent tinea cruris means an untreated reservoir**: the feet, the nails, or another family member.
Groin rash in a person with diabetes: also think of Candida and secondary bacterial infection.
Thick, discoloured toenails with tinea pedis: see [fungal nail infection](condition:onychomycosis) and send clippings before oral treatment.
Scaly rings that fail antifungals: work through the [annular rash differential](condition:annular-rashes).

quiz.q: Where do you take scrapings from in tinea corporis?
How long to continue a topical antifungal?
quiz.a: Until 1–2 weeks after the skin looks clear.

quiz.q: Groin rash involving the scrotum with satellites: tinea or Candida?
quiz.a: Candida. Tinea cruris usually spares the scrotum.

quiz.q: What does a steroid alone do to tinea?
quiz.a: Suppresses local immunity so the fungus spreads: tinea incognito (larger, less scaly, atypical).
